title: The question decides what the workspace holds
takeaway: The same passage, read after two different questions, loads different content into the J-space at the passage's own tokens: a question that requires naming a property (its tense, its part of speech) puts that property's label into the lens readout at several stimulus positions, while a next-word question - which uses the same property without naming it - leaves the label absent. The prior question, not the text, decides what enters the workspace: top-down attention.
walkthrough:
This is a live widget rather than a static image. Each panel shows one trial of the [[paired-question-protocol]]: a question printed first, then a short stimulus passage rendered token by token. A stimulus token is shaded wherever the target property's label - a token such as past or adjective - appears among the top 10 entries of the [[j-lens-readout]] at that position, at any layer. Darker shading means a better rank for the label.

The panels come in pairs. Both panels of a pair contain the identical stimulus passage; only the question before it differs. One question asks the model to predict the passage's next word. Answering it correctly requires being sensitive to some property of the text - its tense, or the part of speech the syntax demands - but never requires naming that property. The other question asks for the property by name, for example "What part of speech do you think the next word will be?". Because the stimulus tokens are the same in both panels, any difference in shading on them is attributable to the question alone.

The pattern the paper reports: under the next-word question the shading is absent - in the part-of-speech example, neither adjective nor adj appears in the readouts, and in the tense example past never appears. Under the name-the-property question the label surfaces at several stimulus positions - three, in the adjective example - and the model then answers correctly.

One control is built into the behavior itself. The next-word predictions respect the property in every case: the model produces an adjective, or a past-tense continuation, even when the label never enters the lens. The property is therefore computed and in use under both questions. What the question modulates is whether its label is loaded into the [[j-space]] - a distinction section 3.5 returns to, between using information automatically and holding it explicitly.

The earlier experiments in this section used explicit instructions ("think about X"). This figure shows [[directed-modulation]] operating without any named concept: the task demand alone, carried forward from the question, redirects which aspect of a fixed input occupies the workspace while the model reads. The paper offers this as the model's analogue of top-down attentional control.

terms.definition: One trial of the protocol: a question followed by the stimulus passage with per-token shading. Panels pair up - same stimulus, different question.
The short text passage the model reads after the question. It is identical across the two panels of a pair, so it cannot be the source of any difference in lens content.
The text placed before the stimulus. One version asks for the passage's next word; the other asks the model to name a property of the text (its tense, the coming word's part of speech).
The single vocabulary token naming the property under test - for example past or adjective. The widget checks for this token in the lens readout at each stimulus position.
The ten highest-scoring vocabulary tokens in the Jacobian lens readout at a given position. A stimulus token is shaded only if the target label is among these ten at some layer there.
The visual encoding: shaded means the target label is in the lens top-10 at that token, and darker shading means the label ranks nearer the top of the readout.
The target label in the tense example. It appears in lens readouts on the stimulus only when the question explicitly asks when the passage's events are set, never under the next-word question.

The target label in the part-of-speech example. Under the naming question it appears at three stimulus positions and the model answers "adjective"; under the next-word question it is absent even though the model's answer, "unacceptable", is an adjective.

numbers.meaning: The rank cutoff for shading: a stimulus token is shaded when the target label is among the top 10 tokens of the J-lens readout at that position. Top-10 is the paper's usual working window for lens presence.

Questions per stimulus - the two conditions of the paired design. Holding the stimulus fixed while varying only the question is what lets any lens difference on stimulus tokens be attributed to the question.

The number of stimulus positions at which adjective-related lens readouts appear under the explicit part-of-speech question, in the first example. The exact count is incidental; what matters is that it is several rather than zero.

The label's appearances under the next-word condition: the paper reports that neither adjective nor adj appears in that example, and that past never appears in the tense example - even though the model's continuation respects the property in every case.
